title-group.article-title: Salivary gland swelling as a characteristic manifestation of local cytokine release syndrome after anti-CD19 chimeric antigen receptor T cell therapy: A case series

abstract.title: Abstract
abstract.p: Cytokine release syndrome (CRS) is the most common adverse event of chimeric antigen receptor T (CAR-T) cell therapy and is usually characterized by systemic symptoms such as fever, hypotension, and hypoxia. However, there have been several recent reports of local CRS characterized by cervical swelling. This localized syndrome can cause life-threatening laryngeal edema and requires early diagnostic treatment. Here we report 3 cases of local CRS where bilateral salivary gland swelling emerged following anti-CD19 CAR-T cell therapy for relapsed or refractory diffuse large B-cell lymphoma. Following tocilizumab treatment for systemic CRS, all patients exhibited cervical swelling. Physical examinations revealed significant swelling of the bilateral submandibular glands, and computed tomography scans showed substantial enlargement of the bilateral parotid and submandibular glands. Immediate treatment with dexamethasone effectively managed the potentially life-threatening laryngeal or pharyngeal edema, thereby preventing severe airway obstruction. This study has demonstrated, for the first time to our knowledge, that salivary gland enlargement is a common finding in local CRS. This observation suggests that physicians should continue to closely monitor the risk of developing cervical edema leading to life-threatening airway obstruction after systemic CRS, even in patients treated with tocilizumab. If salivary gland swelling is observed, it would be better to consider prompt evaluation and dexamethasone administration.

sec.p: Keywords: dexamethasone, malignant lymphoma, salivary gland, cytokine release syndrome, chimeric antigen receptor T cell therapy

sec.title: INTRODUCTION
sec.p: Anti-CD19 chimeric antigen receptor T (CAR-T) cell therapy has dramatically changed the treatment strategy for relapsed or refractory B-cell malignancies.1–3 Although this therapy can provide durable remissions, it also causes several characteristic adverse events. The most common of these, cytokine release syndrome (CRS), is characterized by constitutional symptoms such as fever, hypotension, and hypoxia.4 However, there have been several recent reports of “local CRS” characterized by cervical swelling.5–10 This localized syndrome could cause life-threatening laryngeal edema and requires early diagnostic procedures. Here we report 3 cases where bilateral salivary gland swelling emerged after tocilizumab for prior systemic CRS, and early dexamethasone treatment prevented life-threatening airway obstruction.

sec.title: Case 1
sec.p: A 75-year-old man was diagnosed with stage IVA diffuse large B-cell lymphoma, not otherwise specified (DLBCL-NOS), non-germinal center B-cell-like (non-GCB) type, with involvement of the left axillary lymph node, left scapula, and ileum. After receiving one cycle of R-CHOP11 (rituximab, cyclophosphamide, doxorubicin, vincristine, and prednisolone) as initial treatment and remaining in stable disease (SD), he underwent one cycle of CHASER12 (cyclophosphamide, high-dose cytarabine, dexamethasone, etoposide, and rituximab), leading to a partial response (PR). However, he presented with gastrointestinal tract perforation associated with lymphoma and was unable to receive chemotherapy, resulting in progressive disease (PD) during this period. Consequently, he underwent lymphocyte apheresis for CAR-T cell therapy and then was treated with one cycle of Pola-BR13 (polatuzumab vedotin, bendamustine, and rituximab) and one cycle of CHASER as bridging therapies, resulting in CR. Five months after diagnosis, the patient received lymphocyte-depleting (LD) therapy consisting of fludarabine (Flu) and cyclophosphamide (CY), followed by lisocabtagene maraleucel (Liso-cel) (50 × 106 CD8+ and 50 × 106 CD4+ CAR-positive viable cells). The lactate dehydrogenase (LDH) and ferritin values before LD therapy were 264 U/L (with the upper limit of normal being 222 U/L) and 1486 ng/ml, respectively. In addition, the endothelial activation and stress index (EASIX) score14 was 0.79. The patient had no cervical lesions since diagnosis.

Two days after CAR-T cell infusion, the patient developed a fever exceeding 38°C, categorized as CRS grade 1, and was administered tocilizumab 8 mg/kg. His fever resolved immediately but recurred on day 5. Physical examination revealed significant cervical swelling alongside mild hypoxia with a percutaneous oxygen saturation (SpO2) of 94% (Figure 1A). Computed tomography (CT) showed bilateral parotid and submandibular gland swelling in addition to laryngeal and pharyngeal edema (Figure 1B–D), and blood tests showed a slightly elevated C-reactive protein (CRP) value of 0.88 mg/dL. He was diagnosed with symptoms linked to CRS and was started on a daily dose of 40 mg dexamethasone along with a second dose of tocilizumab 8 mg/kg. Subsequently, his cervical swelling immediately improved and returned to baseline. The dexamethasone was tapered off until discontinuation on day 10, with no recurrence of cervical swelling (Figure 2A).

sec.title: Case 2
sec.p: A 73-year-old man was diagnosed with DLBCL-NOS, GCB type. He presented with a mass extending from the stomach to the duodenum and had lymph node involvement within the abdomen, staged as II according to the Lugano staging system for gastrointestinal tract lymphomas.15 He received one cycle of Pola-R-CHP16 (polatuzumab vedotin, rituximab, cyclophosphamide, doxorubicin, and prednisolone) as a first-line treatment, but his disease worsened. He was then administered one cycle of R-GDP17 (rituximab, gemcitabine, dexamethasone, and cisplatin), but remained in SD. After irradiation for the mass extending from the stomach to the duodenum, the patient underwent lymphocyte apheresis for CAR-T cell therapy. He was administered one cycle of R-DeVIC18 (rituximab, dexamethasone, etoposide, ifosfamide, and carboplatin) as a bridging therapy. However, his disease status remained SD, with residual disease observed in the right axillary, mediastinal, and intra-abdominal lymph nodes, as well as in the spleen. Four months after diagnosis, the patient received Liso-cel (50 × 106 CD8+ and 50 × 106 CD4+ CAR-positive viable cells) after LD therapy consisting of Flu + CY. The LDH and ferritin values before LD therapy were 237 U/L and 268 ng/ml, respectively. In addition, the EASIX score was 1.92. The patient showed no indications of cervical lesions after diagnosis.

The day after CAR-T cell infusion, he developed a fever exceeding 38°C. He was diagnosed as CRS grade 1 and received tocilizumab 8 mg/kg and dexamethasone 10 mg per day. His fever immediately resolved, and the dexamethasone was discontinued on day 3. However, on day 4, he again developed a fever over 38°C, and a physical examination revealed significant cervical edema with mild hypoxia of SpO2 94% (Figure 1E). CT showed bilateral parotid and submandibular gland swelling in addition to pharyngeal edema (Figure 1F–H), and blood tests showed a CRP level of 0.58 mg/dL. He was diagnosed with symptoms linked to CRS and was returned to treatment with dexamethasone 10 mg per day and also received a second dose of tocilizumab 8 mg/kg. The cervical edema immediately improved and returned to baseline, and dexamethasone was tapered and discontinued on day 10 (Figure 2B). Cervical swelling did not recur.

sec.title: Case 3
sec.p: A 71-year-old woman with stage IV DLBCL-NOS, non-GCB type, with left neck and right supraclavicular fossa lymph nodes as well as bone marrow involvement, was administered 6 cycles of R-CHOP as first-line treatment, resulting in CR. However, 6 months after completing therapy, she experienced a recurrence of DLBCL with a new lesion in the right inguinal lymph node. As a response to this relapse, she underwent a treatment regimen comprising one cycle of Pola-BR and four cycles of R-ESHAP19 (rituximab, etoposide, high-dose cytarabine, cisplatin, and methylprednisolone), resulting in CR. However, 6 months after the end of treatment, she was diagnosed with a second relapse of DLBCL, with skin lesions on the right femoral region. After lymphocyte apheresis to prepare for CAR-T cell therapy, she received 2 cycles of Pola-BR as bridging treatments. These procedures led to a PR, although some residual lesions persisted on skin of the right femoral region. Four months after the second relapse, the patient received tisagenlecleucel (Tisa-cel) (4.5 × 108 CAR-positive viable cells) after undergoing LD therapy consisting of Flu + CY. The LDH and ferritin values before LD therapy were 430 U/L and 310 ng/ml, respectively. In addition, the EASIX score was 1.81. The patient had no cervical lesions since diagnosis.

On day 2 after CAR-T cell infusion, she developed a fever exceeding 38°C and was diagnosed with CRS grade 1, and received tocilizumab 8 mg/kg. Her fever immediately resolved, but she again developed a fever of more than 38°C with significant cervical edema on day 4 (Figure 1I). She was not hypoxic but did exhibit hoarseness. CT showed bilateral parotid and submandibular gland swelling in addition to laryngeal and pharyngeal edema (Figure 1J–L), and a blood test showed a CRP value of 0.22 mg/dL. The patient was diagnosed with cervical swelling associated with CRS and was started on dexamethasone 40 mg per day. Her hoarseness and cervical edema immediately improved to baseline. The dexamethasone was tapered off until discontinuation on day 9 (Figure 2C). Cervical swelling did not recur.

sec.title: DISCUSSION
sec.p: We experienced 3 cases of local CRS characterized by cervical swelling. All patients exhibited enlarged salivary glands and potentially fatal laryngeal or pharyngeal edema, but early administration of dexamethasone resulted in rapid recovery without significant respiratory impairment.

CRS is one of the most common adverse events after CAR-T cell therapy. CRS usually presents with systemic symptoms, and the American Society for Transplantation and Cellular Therapy (ASTCT) consensus includes a grading scale that assesses CRS according to systemic symptoms such as fever, hypotension, and hypoxia.4

On the other hand, CRS characterized by local symptoms has recently been reported. Wei et al. reported several cases of erythema, swelling, and enlargement at the site of lymphoma infiltration and around lesions in the inguinal and cervicofacial regions, and described this localized inflammation as local CRS.20 In a subsequent case report, a patient diagnosed with DLBCL initially presenting with a cervical lymphoma lesion experienced rapid enlargement of the lesion and developed severe dyspnea following CAR-T cell infusion.5 Thus, local CRS was initially assumed to be a localized inflammatory reaction at the tumor site, which precedes systemic CRS and is directly attacked by CAR-T cells.

However, several cases of cervical edema in B-cell acute lymphoblastic leukemia (B-ALL)6,7,9 and DLBCL8 patients after anti-CD19 CAR-T therapy have been reported despite the administration of tocilizumab for prior systemic CRS. A comparable situation has been documented more recently in anti-B cell maturation antigen (BCMA) CAR-T cell therapy for multiple myeloma10 (Table 1). There are several common features among these cases, including ours. Even patients without cervical mass lesions developed local CRS characterized by cervical edema, and in all but one case, local CRS developed after the administration of tocilizumab for prior systemic CRS and improved immediately upon intravenous administration of dexamethasone.

sec.p: Tocilizumab, an interleukin-6 (IL-6) receptor antagonist, is the first-line treatment for systemic CRS,21 but its efficacy in local CRS is unknown. All of our patients developed local CRS despite having previously received tocilizumab for systemic CRS. Furthermore, the CRP values were low at the onset of local CRS, suggesting that tocilizumab adequately suppressed IL-6. These findings suggested that the cytokine response in local CRS may be different from that in systemic CRS. Further studies are needed to clarify the pathogenesis of local CRS.

In our 3 cases, CT showed significant enlargement of bilateral parotid and submandibular glands; the same findings were observed on CT in previously reported cases of B-ALL9 and DLBCL.8 Early diagnosis and intervention of local CRS with laryngeal edema are very important to prevent fatal airway obstruction. Direct observation of laryngeal edema requires laryngeal fiberscope, a procedure that might not be promptly accessible. In this study, we identified bilateral submandibular gland enlargement during physical examinations and bilateral parotid and submandibular glands on CT scans as typical signs of local CRS. These observations prompted early intervention with dexamethasone, averting serious airway obstruction.

There has been limited knowledge about local CRS. At our institution, 104 patients had received anti-CD19 CAR-T cell therapy by March 2024, and 3 of them developed local CRS. However, a larger number of cases is needed to determine the exact incidence. While ferritin levels and EASIX scores before LD therapy have been associated with the development of systemic CRS,14 our study did not find a correlation between these values and local CRS. In addition, the management of CRS after CAR-T cell therapy at our institution followed the National Comprehensive Cancer Network (NCCN) guidelines,22 but the dose of dexamethasone for cervical edema was determined at the physician’s discretion. Further case accumulation is necessary to establish the appropriate dexamethasone dosage for local CRS.

We experienced 3 cases of cervical edema after the onset of systemic CRS in anti-CD19 CAR-T cell therapy, despite the absence of cervical lesions. All patients had significant bilateral salivary gland swelling and could be managed with immediate dexamethasone administration without causing severe airway obstruction. Physicians should continue to closely monitor the risk of developing cervical edema leading to life-threatening airway obstruction even after tocilizumab for systemic CRS and consider prompt evaluation and dexamethasone administration if salivary gland swelling is observed.
